query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys in the form of nanoscale thin films or lithographically patterned nanoribbons, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles, given that the notable response reported for bulk forms may not persist in a genuinely low-dimensional state and that heat-transfer rate limits cycle frequency? Specify one controlled intervention, predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, applicable operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA nanoscale films and nanoribbons, the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles are governed by finite-size effects that enhance interfacial strain and magnetic anisotropy. These effects cause increased domain pinning and coercivity relative to bulk forms, while the reduced dimensions also create heat-transfer limitations that further modify the dynamic cooling response.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA with a nanocrystalline morphology in thin film or lithographically patterned nanoribbon form
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition thermal annealing treatment combined with engineering the substrate interface (using high thermal conductivity substrates) to alleviate interfacial strain and improve heat transfer
generation.conditions: Low-applied magnetic fields (up to ~4 T) at temperatures around the alloy’s Curie temperature, under magnetic-cooling cycle conditions where heat transfer rate limitations become significant
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale grain boundaries and interfacial regions that introduce enhanced magnetoelastic strain and modified magnetic domain configurations
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale dimensions produce enhanced interface- and surface-driven strain that increases magnetic anisotropy and domain pinning. This in turn elevates the coercive field and reduces the maximum magnetic entropy change compared with bulk forms. Additionally, the limited heat-transfer rate typical of nanoscale samples further hinders the dynamic response during rapid cooling cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples and those fabricated on high thermal conductivity substrates will show a modest increase in maximum magnetic entropy change and a reduction in hysteresis (i.e. lower coercivity). Improved heat transfer should also yield less temperature lag during dynamic cycle frequencies, though the improvement may not fully match bulk material performance.
generation.baseline: As-deposited nanoscale HEA films/nanoribbons exhibit lower maximum entropy change and increased coercivity (indicative of larger hysteresis losses) compared to bulk samples, partly owing to finite-size and interfacial effects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoscale samples fabricated by methods such as physical vapor deposition or lithographic patterning under low-to-moderate applied field conditions and near the alloy’s magnetic ordering temperature. Extreme annealing conditions or alternative geometries outside this range could lead to phase changes or different microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of strain relaxation on the magnetic domain reconfiguration and the magnitude of heat-transfer improvement remains uncertain without targeted experimental assessments.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA nanoscale samples: one set remains as-deposited, and the other set undergoes controlled thermal annealing and is deposited on high thermal conductivity substrates. Subject both sets to low-field magnetic-cooling cycles around the Curie temperature while recording magnetization hysteresis loops and temperature profiles.
measurements: Maximum magnetic entropy change (ΔS) from magnetic isotherms
Cycle-induced temperature distributions using thermal imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed/high-conductivity substrate samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis (lower Hc) and an increase in maximum ΔS relative to the as-deposited samples, or if improved heat-transfer does not lead to reduced temperature lag during cycling, then the hypothesis attributing the altered magnetocaloric response to finite-size strain and heat-transfer limitations is falsified.

It is noteworthy that, generally, polycrystalline samples exhibit higher maximum entropy change −ΔSM compared to their nano-sized counterparts, as seen in Figure 10a vs. 10b. Bulk compound with x = 0.05 shows −ΔSM (max) = 5.56 J/kgK at 4 T and nano-sized sample shows −ΔSM (max) = 3.25 J/kgK at 4 T. Bulk samples with x = 0.1 and x = 0.2 exhibit high maximum entropy change at 6.9 J/kgK and 9.2 J/kgK respectively. For all samples, maximum entropy change occurs at around their Curie temperature TC. It is also important to note that nanocrystalline compounds exhibit wider range of effective temperature δTFWHM at around 40–70 K while bulk samples show range of 20–30 K. chosen.approach: Characterization study comparing nano versus bulk magnetocaloric properties
